title: Approval and Promulgation of Implementation Plans; State of Utah; Salt Lake City and Provo, Utah PM2.5 Redesignations to Attainment and Utah State Implementation Plan Revisions
summary:
The Environmental Protection Agency has officially moved Salt Lake City and Provo, Utah from “nonattainment” to “attainment” for the 24-hour standard for fine particle pollution, and approved Utah’s long-term plans to keep the air clean. The decision takes effect December 19, 2025.

What’s changing: Utah’s updated air plans are now part of the federal record. They include maintenance plans through 2035, limits that guide how much pollution cars and trucks can add as transportation projects move forward, and source-specific requirements for major facilities. The package also updates several state rules and adjusts certain limits at the Kennecott power plant. In short, the state documented that air quality has improved based on 2022–2024 data and laid out how it will stay on track.

Who benefits: Residents along the Wasatch Front stand to gain the most from cleaner winter air and fewer high-pollution days. Health systems and schools may see fewer pollution-related illnesses and absences. State and local agencies get regulatory certainty, which helps transportation planners align road and transit investments with clean air goals. Businesses also gain clarity from a stable, federally approved plan and the positive signal that comes with an attainment designation.

Who may have concerns: Some industries and fleets will continue investing in cleaner technologies and practices to meet the controls Utah committed to, which can carry costs. Clean air advocates may worry about backsliding if growth outpaces planned reductions, or about specific rule changes like the adjustment at Kennecott. Communities will watch closely to ensure the maintenance plans are enforced and updated as needed. The rule does not change how air programs apply on reservation lands.

Two smaller actions accompanied this decision. EPA updated a Maricopa County, Arizona dry cleaning rule into the federal plan, a housekeeping step that makes the local rule federally enforceable. And NOAA issued a technical correction to a halibut charter fee rule in Alaska to add a missing definition; it aligns the regulation with what was already announced and does not change policy.
